title: Optimal n for $L^d_n$-list-colorability
statement_text: Fixing $d$, what is the optimal value of $n$ such that $[n]^d$ is $L^d_n$-list-colorable?
context_text: Here $[n]^d=\{1,\dots,n\}^d$ is viewed as an induced subgraph of the lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ (two points adjacent iff they differ by $1$ in exactly one coordinate). For a graph $G$ and $L:V(G)\to\mathbb{N}$, $G$ is $L$-list-colorable if for every choice of lists $S_v$ with $|S_v|\ge L(v)$ there is a proper coloring $f$ with $f(v)\in S_v$ for all $v$. The function $L_n^d:[n]^d\to\{2,\dots,d+2\}$ is $L_n^d(i_1,\dots,i_d)=2+|\{k: 1<i_k<n\}|$, i.e. two plus the number of coordinates that are not on the boundary of the box. The authors prove that $[n]^d$ is $L_n^d$-list-colorable whenever $n\ge d+2$; consequently, for $q\ge d+2$ colors any partial proper $q$-coloring of the boundary of a box of side $n\ge d+2$ extends to the whole box, which is used to classify the mixing properties of proper $q$-colorings of $\mathbb{Z}^d$. The property is monotone: if $[n]^d$ is $L_n^d$-list-colorable then so are $[n]^{d-1}$ (with $L_n^{d-1}$) and $[n+1]^d$ (with $L_{n+1}^d$), which justifies asking for the smallest such $n$. The threshold $d+2$ is not always optimal: $[2]^2$ is $L_2^2$-list-colorable although $2<4$, while $[2]^3$ is not $L_2^3$-list-colorable. The authors did not try to optimise $n$.
notes: Stated in running prose: 'Fixing d, the question of the optimal value of n such that [n]^d is L^d_n-list-colorable remains.' Section 5 (not fully reproduced in the extracted text) apparently contains additional formal open questions including a labeled Question 5.7 concerning whether $[n]^2$ is $\min\{L^2_n, 3\}$-list-colorable; its full statement could not be extracted.
paper_title: Mixing properties of colorings of the $\mathbb{Z}^d$ lattice
